title: Geometry-Only CSL/DP Ratios and the Nonuniqueness of Decoherence Kernels
abstract: We study idealized levitated protocols that create spatial superpositions of massive test particles. For each protocol, we compare the dimensionless contrast-loss exponent of mass-proportional continuous spontaneous localization (CSL) with the Diósi--Penrose (DP) self-energy exponent $E_Gτ/\hbar$. We first prove that the point-particle CSL separation kernel has an exact random-unitary realization: Gaussian momentum kicks arriving at Poisson-distributed times produce the same unconditional decay of spatial coherence, although a pure state conditioned on the complete kick record remains pure. The separation kernel alone therefore specifies an operational decoherence law, not the occurrence of objective collapse. We then show that the ratio of the CSL and DP exponents is independent of particle mass and interrogation time. In the point-particle model it depends only on branch separation and an effective distance; for the standard GRW reference parameters, its resolved-superposition crossover is $x_*\approx1.91\,\mathrm{nm}$. For rigid spherical bodies with an arbitrary normalized radial mass profile, total mass, overall density scale, and interrogation time again cancel, leaving a dimensionless geometry factor. The results distinguish three requirements for a decisive experiment: detectable absolute effects, a controlled comparison of CSL and DP scales, and observables capable of discriminating physically different dynamics that share the same ensemble decoherence kernel.
summary: This paper theoretically compares the decoherence predictions of Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) and Diósi–Penrose (DP) theories using massive particle superpositions. The key finding is that the ratio between their respective exponents simplifies to a geometry-only factor, independent of mass or time. This provides a powerful framework for designing experiments capable of distinguishing between these fundamental models of quantum gravity effects.
main_problem: The paper compares two theoretical predictions for decoherence—Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) and Diósi–Penrose (DP)—by analyzing the ratio of their respective contrast-loss exponents.
main_result: The ratio of these exponents ($\Xi_{	ext{CSL/DP}}$) is found to be independent of particle mass and interrogation time, depending only on geometric factors derived from the superposition separation and particle shape.
method: The authors use theoretical derivations involving master equations, random-unitary realizations, and Fourier analysis applied to finite spherical density profiles to establish conversion theorems between the two decoherence models.
model_or_system: The study focuses on idealized levitated protocols creating spatial superpositions of massive test particles, modeled using point-particle approximations and generalized to rigid spherically symmetric bodies with arbitrary mass profiles.
key_observables: The dimensionless ratio $\Xi_{	ext{CSL/DP}}$ (the ratio of CSL and DP exponents), the resolved-superposition crossover distance ($x^*$), and the profile amplification factor $A_{\varrho}$.
important_parameters: Branch separation ($\Delta x$), particle radius ($R$), interrogation time ($	au$), CSL localization length ($r_C$), and the geometry factor derived from mass distribution.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that ensemble visibility loss is equivalent to decoherence, but cautions that this does not prove objective collapse because pure states remain pure conditioned on the full kick record.
figures_summary: Figures numerically evaluate the identity relating CSL and DP derived exponents for various protocols and plot how the ratio changes based on geometry factors for different mass profiles.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the point-particle case, proving the random-unitary realization of CSL. It then generalizes this to finite spherical bodies using Fourier analysis to derive a universal conversion theorem for the exponent ratio, concluding with discussions on experimental observability and limitations.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical tools to compare competing objective collapse models (CSL vs DP) by reducing their comparison to purely geometric ratios, which is crucial for designing future high-precision quantum experiments in AMO physics.
